prompt: What kinds of strain does the chair conformation of cyclohexane have?

choices.text: Neither angle strain nor torsional strain
Angle strain only
choices.why: All of the chair's C−C−C bond angles are near the 109° tetrahedral value, so it has no angle strain.

choices.text: Torsional strain only
choices.why: All neighboring C−H bonds in the chair are staggered, so it has no torsional strain.

choices.text: Both steric strain and torsional strain
choices.why: That describes the twist-boat conformation, which lies about 23 kJ/mol above the chair.

explanation: Cyclohexane adopts a strain-free chair conformation: all C−C−C bond angles are near the 109° tetrahedral value, and all neighboring C−H bonds are staggered (Figure 4.5.1).

prompt: What is the C−C−C bond angle in chair cyclohexane, in degrees?
explanation: All C−C−C bond angles in chair cyclohexane are 111.5°, close to the ideal 109° tetrahedral angle (Figure 4.5.1).

prompt: By how many degrees does the C−C−C bond angle of chair cyclohexane (111.5°) differ from the 109° tetrahedral value the section compares it with?
explanation: 111.5° − 109° = 2.5°. That is close enough to tetrahedral that chair cyclohexane is described as having no angle strain.

prompt: How are neighboring C−H bonds arranged in chair cyclohexane?

choices.text: All of them are staggered
All of them are eclipsed
choices.why: Eclipsed C−H bonds would cause torsional strain, and the chair has none.

choices.text: Half are staggered and half are eclipsed
choices.why: The chair is strain-free because every pair of neighboring C−H bonds is staggered, as the Newman projection in Figure 4.5.1 shows.

choices.text: Most are nearly staggered, but a few remain eclipsed
choices.why: That is closer to cyclopentane. In chair cyclohexane all neighboring C−H bonds are staggered.

explanation: In chair cyclohexane all neighboring C−H bonds are staggered, so it has no torsional strain (Figure 4.5.1).

prompt: About how much higher in energy is the twist-boat conformation of cyclohexane than the chair conformation, in kJ/mol?
explanation: The twist-boat conformation is about 23 kJ/mol (5.5 kcal/mol) higher in energy than the chair conformation, so molecules adopt it only rarely.

prompt: Which kinds of strain does the twist-boat conformation of cyclohexane have?

choices.text: Steric strain and torsional strain, but it is nearly free of angle strain
Angle strain only
choices.why: The twist-boat is nearly free of angle strain; its extra energy comes from steric and torsional strain.

choices.text: Angle strain and torsional strain, but no steric strain
choices.why: The section says the twist-boat is nearly free of angle strain and has both steric and torsional strain.

choices.text: No strain at all, the same as the chair
choices.why: The twist-boat is about 23 kJ/mol higher in energy than the strain-free chair.

explanation: The twist-boat conformation is nearly free of angle strain. It does, however, have both steric strain and torsional strain and is about 23 kJ/mol (5.5 kcal/mol) higher in energy than the chair.

prompt: Why do cyclohexane molecules adopt the twist-boat geometry only rarely?

choices.text: It is about 23 kJ/mol higher in energy than the chair conformation
It has severe angle strain
choices.why: The twist-boat is nearly free of angle strain. Its higher energy comes from steric and torsional strain.

choices.text: It cannot exist because its bond angles are impossible
choices.why: The twist-boat is a real conformation of cyclohexane; it is simply less stable than the chair.

choices.text: It is lower in energy, but the chair forms faster
choices.why: The chair is the lower-energy conformation; the twist-boat lies about 23 kJ/mol above it.

explanation: The twist-boat has both steric and torsional strain and is about 23 kJ/mol (5.5 kcal/mol) higher in energy than the strain-free chair. As a result, molecules adopt the twist-boat geometry only rarely.

prompt: When you draw a chair cyclohexane, the first step is two parallel, slightly offset lines. How many of the ring's carbons do these lines place in one plane?
explanation: Step 1 is to draw two parallel lines, slanted downward and slightly offset from each other, which means that four of the cyclohexane carbons lie in a plane. The other two carbons go above and below that plane.

prompt: In drawing a chair cyclohexane, where do the two remaining carbons go relative to the plane of the middle four?

choices.text: The topmost carbon above and to the right; the bottommost carbon below and to the left
Both above the plane, one at each end
choices.why: In the chair, the two end carbons go on opposite sides: one above the plane of the middle four and one below it.

choices.text: The topmost carbon above and to the left; the bottommost carbon below and to the right
choices.why: The section's procedure puts the topmost carbon above and to the right and the bottommost below and to the left.

choices.text: Both in the same plane as the other four
choices.why: That would be a flat hexagon. The chair has one carbon above and one below the plane of the middle four.

explanation: Step 2 places the topmost carbon above and to the right of the plane of the other four; step 3 places the bottommost carbon below and to the left of the plane of the middle four.

prompt: In a correctly drawn chair cyclohexane, how are the bonds to the bottommost carbon related to the bonds to the topmost carbon?

choices.text: They are parallel
They are perpendicular
choices.why: The section's drawing procedure notes that the bonds to the bottommost carbon are parallel to those to the topmost carbon.

choices.text: They point toward each other
choices.why: The end carbons sit on opposite sides of the plane of the middle four, and their bonds run parallel.

choices.text: They lie in the same plane as the middle four carbons
choices.why: The topmost and bottommost carbons are placed above and below the plane of the middle four, so their bonds leave that plane.

explanation: In step 3 of drawing a chair, the bottommost carbon is placed below and to the left of the plane of the middle four, and the bonds to it are parallel to the bonds to the topmost carbon.

prompt: In the book's drawings of chair cyclohexane, which bond is nearer the viewer?

choices.text: The lower bond, drawn heavily shaded
The upper bond, drawn heavily shaded
choices.why: By the book's convention the upper bond is in back. The shaded front bond is the lower one.

choices.text: Neither; all bonds in a chair are the same distance from the viewer
choices.why: The chair is three-dimensional, and the drawing has a front and a back.

choices.text: Whichever bond is drawn longest
choices.why: Nearness is shown by heavy shading of the lower bond, not by bond length.

explanation: When viewing cyclohexane, it's helpful to remember that the lower bond is in front and the upper bond is in back. The book draws the front (lower) bond heavily shaded to indicate nearness to the viewer.

prompt: Which cycloalkanes are the most common and occur most widely in nature?

choices.text: Substituted cyclohexanes
Substituted cyclopropanes
choices.why: Steroids, many pharmaceutical agents, and menthol all contain six-membered rings, not three-membered ones.

choices.text: Substituted cyclobutanes
choices.why: The section names substituted cyclohexanes as the most common cycloalkanes.

choices.text: Unsubstituted cyclopentane
choices.why: The section names substituted cyclohexanes as the most common, found in steroids and many pharmaceutical agents.

explanation: Substituted cyclohexanes are the most common cycloalkanes and occur widely in nature. Steroids and many pharmaceutical agents have cyclohexane rings.

prompt: How many substituents does the flavoring agent menthol have on its six-membered ring?
explanation: Menthol, a flavoring agent, has three substituents on a six-membered ring. It is one example of the many natural compounds with cyclohexane rings.
